cards.front: What are the six main factors in material selection?
cards.answer: Functionality / Aesthetics / Availability / Cost / Environmental impact / Social & ethical considerations

cards.front: Why does ease of working affect how much a material costs to manufacture with?
cards.answer: If a material is difficult to cut, shape or join, production costs rise.

cards.front: Why do exotic hardwoods such as ebony raise sustainability concerns despite their attractive appearance?
cards.answer: They are rare, which drives up their cost and raises sustainability concerns.

cards.front: What are the five key systems used in modern manufacturing?
cards.answer: CAD / CAM / FMS / JIT / Lean manufacturing

cards.front: What three benefits does automation bring to manufacturing?
cards.answer: Increases production speed / Improves consistency / Reduces labour costs

cards.front: Why does crowd funding reduce a designer's financial risk before manufacturing begins?
cards.answer: Crowd funding raises money from customers before manufacturing begins, removing the need for bank loans or investors.

cards.front: Why do ethical designers focus on repairability and maintenance rather than planned obsolescence?
cards.answer: Planned obsolescence generates repeat sales but creates waste, so ethical designers extend a product's full lifecycle instead.

cards.front: Why do designers usually carry out secondary research before primary research?
cards.answer: Secondary research builds background knowledge quickly and cheaply, and primary research then fills any remaining gaps.

cards.front: Why might a designer modify their design brief partway through a project?
cards.answer: Research often reveals new information, and revising the brief is a normal part of the iterative design process.

cards.front: What are the five main renewable energy sources?
cards.answer: Wind / Solar / Tidal / Hydroelectric / Biomass

cards.front: What are three arguments against continuing to rely on fossil fuels for energy?
items: Finite resources that will run out
Release greenhouse gases, causing climate change
cards.answer: Finite resources that will run out / Release greenhouse gases, causing climate change / Extraction damages habitats

cards.front: How does a nuclear power station use nuclear fission to generate electricity?
cards.answer: Splitting uranium atoms in nuclear fission releases heat that turns water to steam, driving the turbines.

cards.front: Why can a pumped storage system generate electricity almost instantly when demand rises?
cards.answer: Stored water is released downhill through turbines, generating electricity almost immediately.

cards.front: What are the five types of force that can act on a product in use?
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Bending / Torsion / Shear

cards.front: What are the four common methods used to reinforce or stiffen materials?
cards.answer: Lamination / Folding / Webbing / Fabric interfacing

cards.front: Why does corrugated card resist compression well?
cards.answer: Its fluted inner layer acts as a series of small arches, resisting the squashing force.

cards.front: Why can acrylic shatter under impact while polypropylene flexes instead of snapping?
cards.answer: Polypropylene is a flexible thermoplastic that bends to absorb bending forces, while rigid acrylic cannot flex and shatters instead.

cards.front: What are the 6 Rs of sustainability?
cards.answer: Reduce / Reuse / Recycle / Refuse / Rethink / Repair

cards.front: What three challenges must designers consider that link the environment, climate and fair trade?
cards.answer: Deforestation / Rising carbon dioxide levels / The need for fair trade

cards.front: Why does market competition constrain how designers price a new product?
cards.answer: The price must compete against existing products while still covering the cost of quality and features.

cards.front: Why might a designer still choose fair trade materials even though they cost more?
cards.answer: Fair trade materials appeal to ethically conscious consumers and reduce exploitation in the supply chain.

cards.front: What four processes cause the main ecological issues in raw material extraction?
cards.answer: Deforestation (timber) / Mining (metals and minerals) / Drilling (crude oil for polymers) / Farming (cotton and natural fibres)

cards.front: What are the six Rs of sustainable design?
cards.answer: Reduce / Refuse / Re-use / Repair / Recycle / Rethink

cards.front: Why can a cotton T-shirt rack up thousands of product miles before it reaches a customer?
cards.answer: Its cotton may be grown, spun, dyed and assembled in different countries before being sold in another.

cards.front: Why do designers use Fairtrade materials, FSC-certified timber or conflict-free minerals?
cards.answer: To make sure raw material supply chains do not exploit workers or communities.

cards.front: What are the six material categories designers work with?
cards.answer: Papers and boards / Timber-based materials / Metal-based materials / Polymers / Textile-based materials / Electronic and mechanical systems

cards.front: Why is Philippe Starck's approach to design seen as the opposite of William Morris's?
cards.answer: Starck embraces mass production, believing good design should be affordable and accessible to everyone, while Morris championed handcraftsmanship.

cards.front: Why did the Suez fuel crisis push Issigonis toward an innovative small-car design?
cards.answer: It demanded a small, fuel-efficient, affordable car, and this constraint drove his creative engineering solution.

cards.front: What are the three key modern materials, each developed through improved manufacturing processes?
cards.answer: Graphene / Metal foams / Titanium

cards.front: What three types of smart material change their behaviour in response to a stimulus?
cards.answer: Shape memory alloys / Thermochromic pigments / Photochromic pigments

cards.front: Why is graphene suited to applications like flexible screens and ultra-fast electronics?
cards.answer: It is extremely strong, lightweight, flexible, and conducts both heat and electricity very well.

cards.front: Why are metal foams useful for crash protection in vehicles?
cards.answer: They are lightweight but strong, and absorb energy well when impacted.

cards.front: What are the five stages of a life cycle assessment, in order?
cards.answer: Raw material extraction / Processing & manufacture / Distribution & transport / Use & maintenance / End-of-life disposal

cards.front: What are the three main sources of textile fibres?
cards.answer: Animal (wool, silk) / Vegetable (cotton, linen) / Chemical/synthetic (polyester, nylon)

cards.front: Why does recycled paper lose quality after being reprocessed multiple times?
cards.answer: Each recycling cycle shortens the paper's cellulose fibres, which reduces its quality.

cards.front: Why might improving a kettle's insulation cut its environmental impact more than using a lighter plastic casing?
cards.answer: If most of a kettle's impact comes from the energy used to boil water, better insulation matters more than material weight.

cards.front: What are the three stages of the input-process-output model, in order?
cards.answer: Input / Process / Output

cards.front: What three roles can a microcontroller be programmed to perform?
cards.answer: Counter / Timer / Decision maker

cards.front: How does a security light use the input-process-output model to switch itself on and off?
cards.answer: A motion sensor provides the input, a microcontroller decides to switch on the lamp as output, then a timer switches it off later.

cards.front: Why is understanding the input-process-output model useful when designing an electronic product?
cards.answer: It helps you design products that respond automatically to changes in their environment.

cards.front: What are the five design strategies for generating and developing ideas?
cards.answer: Collaboration / User-centred design / Systems approach / Iterative design / Avoiding design fixation

cards.front: Why does gathering data through interviews and usability testing reduce a designer's risk of failure?
cards.answer: It ensures the product is designed around real user needs, reducing the risk of something that looks good but fails in practice.

cards.front: Why do designers build physical models from card, foam or breadboard circuits instead of relying only on drawings?
cards.answer: Physical models test form, proportion and ergonomics in ways that drawings cannot.

cards.front: What are the four types of motion produced by mechanical devices?
cards.answer: Linear motion / Rotary motion / Reciprocating motion / Oscillating motion

cards.front: What are the three classes of lever?
cards.answer: First-order / Second-order / Third-order

cards.front: Why does a bicycle brake lever need a bell crank linkage to work?
cards.answer: The bell crank converts the pulling motion of the lever into a pushing motion that presses the brake pad onto the wheel rim.

cards.front: Why does a second-order lever always multiply force while a third-order lever always multiplies distance and speed?
cards.answer: In a second-order lever the effort moves further than the load; in a third-order lever the load moves further than the effort.

cards.front: What three properties is paper and board measured by when specifying stock?
cards.answer: Thickness (microns or mm) / Weight (grams per square metre) / Colour

cards.front: What three standard components are used to fasten, seal or bind paper and card products?
cards.answer: Fasteners (staples, paper clips) / Seals (adhesive strips) / Bindings (spiral, saddle stitch)

cards.front: Why does efficient nesting matter more in mass production than in making a single item?
cards.answer: Even small material savings per unit add up across thousands of items in batch or mass production.

cards.front: Why is it useful for a designer to know a material's stock forms before placing an order?
cards.answer: It helps them calculate how much material to order, minimise waste and manufacture the product efficiently.

cards.front: What six qualities must a well-developed prototype have?
items: Respond to client wants and needs
cards.answer: Satisfy the brief / Respond to client wants and needs / Demonstrate innovation / Be functional / Consider aesthetics / Be potentially marketable

cards.front: What three things should a designer do when evaluating a prototype?
items: Reflect critically and respond to feedback
cards.answer: Reflect critically and respond to feedback / Suggest modifications to improve it / Assess fitness for purpose

cards.front: Why might a product handle that feels comfortable to its designer still fail some users?
cards.answer: It might be sized to suit the designer's own hands, which can be too small for users with larger hands.

cards.front: Why is the design specification useful as a checklist when evaluating a prototype?
cards.answer: It lists testable criteria, such as dimensions, weight, materials, function and aesthetics, to test the prototype against.

cards.front: What are the four scales of production?
cards.answer: Prototype / Batch / Mass / Continuous

cards.front: What four factors help a designer choose the right scale of production?
cards.answer: Number of products needed / Acceptable unit cost / Level of customisation required / Available budget for tooling

cards.front: How is quality control built into a mass-production assembly line?
cards.answer: Automated sensors check dimensions, weight and surface finish as products move along the line.

cards.front: Why can't a continuous production process like a blast furnace simply be switched off overnight?
cards.answer: Stopping and restarting a continuous process is extremely expensive, and it could damage equipment or waste materials.

cards.front: What are the five main material categories designers choose from?
cards.answer: Papers and boards / Timbers / Metals / Polymers / Textiles

cards.front: What are the six working properties that describe how a material behaves under force?
cards.answer: Strength / Hardness / Toughness / Malleability / Ductility / Elasticity

cards.front: Why is plywood strong in all directions rather than just along the grain?
cards.answer: Its veneer layers are glued with the grain running at right angles to each other.

cards.front: Why is steel coated with zinc in a process called galvanising?
cards.answer: Zinc coats the steel to prevent it from rusting.

cards.front: What three factors is material selection based on?
cards.answer: Functional need / Cost / Availability

cards.front: What five marking-out methods help designers work within tolerances?
cards.answer: Reference datum points / Coordinates / Templates / Jigs / Patterns

cards.front: Why must a saw blade's kerf be factored into cutting measurements?
cards.answer: A saw blade removes a kerf width of material as it cuts, so this must be allowed for in measurements.

cards.front: Why is minimising waste when cutting materials both an economic and an environmental concern?
cards.answer: Wasted material is wasted money, and using less material also means a smaller environmental footprint.

cards.front: What five factors determine which surface finish is chosen for a product?
cards.answer: Material category / Product's environment (indoor/outdoor, wet/dry) / Desired appearance / Cost / Whether it must be food-safe

cards.front: What four surface finishes protect metals from corrosion?
cards.answer: Dip coating / Powder coating / Galvanising / Anodising

cards.front: Why is UV varnishing applied to magazine covers and product boxes?
cards.answer: It makes colours look more vibrant and makes the surface more durable.

cards.front: Why would an outdoor product need a different finish from a food-contact product?
cards.answer: Outdoor products need UV and weather resistance, while food-contact products need non-toxic, food-grade coatings.

cards.front: What are the four manufacturing process categories, based on how they shape material?
cards.answer: Wastage (material removed) / Addition (material joined) / Deforming (material reshaped) / Reforming (material melted and reshaped)

cards.front: What five workshop safety essentials should always be followed when using machinery?
items: Secure workpieces with clamps or vices
No loose clothing, jewellery or untied hair
cards.answer: Wear appropriate PPE / Secure workpieces with clamps or vices / Never leave machines running unattended / Keep guards in place / No loose clothing, jewellery or untied hair

cards.front: Why does laser cutting produce cleaner edges than many other cutting methods?
cards.answer: A focused laser beam cuts sheet material with extremely high precision, leaving minimal kerf.

cards.front: Why is 3D printing well suited to making complex shapes that traditional methods struggle with?
cards.answer: It builds shapes layer by layer, so it can create complex geometries that traditional methods struggle to produce.
